subject: math
title: Likelihood of Simulated Events: More Likely, Less Likely or Equally Likely
seo_title: Grade 3 Math Likelihood and Probability Worksheets (BC Curriculum, Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: Likelihood of simulated events, using comparative language
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 math worksheets on likelihood for the BC curriculum: impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely and certain, more likely and less likely with spinners and bags, tally results from coin and spinner simulations, predictions compared with results, and fair games. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: The bigger the part of the spinner or bag, the more likely the outcome.
key_sub: Compare the size of each part, not the number of sections. Likely is not certain, and unlikely is not impossible. Real results are close to the prediction, not exactly the same.
body_html:
Words for how likely something is

Likelihood tells us how likely something is to happen. Impossible means it can never happen. Certain means it must happen. Unlikely means it could happen, but probably will not. Likely means it will probably happen. Equally likely means two things have the same chance.

WordMeaningExample
impossiblecan never happenAn orca will walk down the street.
unlikelycould happen, but probably will notA black bear will walk onto the school field.
equally likelythe same chanceA tossed coin lands on heads or on tails.
likelywill probably happenIt will rain in Vancouver in November.
certainmust happenWednesday will come after Tuesday.

To compare two events, say which one is more likely or less likely, or say they are equally likely.

Spinners and bags: look at the size of each part

A spinner is more likely to land on a colour that covers more of it. Compare the size of the parts, not just the number of sections. In a bag, the colour with more counters is more likely.

Example

Which colour is the arrow most likely to land on?

Red is one big section: half of the spinner. The 3 small blue sections together are only a quarter.

Answer: red

Simulations and tally results

A simulation uses a coin, spinner, bag or number cube to act out a real event. For example, heads can stand for a goal and tails for a miss. Record each result with a tally mark.

Example

How many spins were not red?

Not red means blue or yellow: 7 + 4 = 11.

Answer: 11 spins

Compare predictions with results

Predict first. If red is 1 of 4 equal sections, predict red about 1 time in every 4 spins. Then compare. Results vary, so they are usually close to the prediction, not exactly the same.

Example

Red is half of a spinner. Kai spins 20 times and gets red 9 times. Was the prediction of about 10 good?

Half of 20 is 10. 9 is close to 10.

Answer: yes, the result is close

Fair games

A game is fair when every player is equally likely to win. A spinner with 2 red and 2 blue equal sections is fair for a red player and a blue player. A number cube game is fair when each player has the same number of faces.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting sections, not their sizeCompare how much of the spinner each colour covers
Saying certain when it is only likelyCertain means it must happen every time. If it could fail, it is likely
Saying impossible when it is only unlikelyIf it could happen even once, it is not impossible
Expecting results to match the prediction exactlyResults vary: close to the prediction is normal
Thinking tails is due after many headsA coin does not remember: heads and tails stay equally likely

faq.q: What do Grade 3 students learn about probability in BC?
faq.a: In the Data and probability area of the BC Grade 3 math curriculum, students describe the likelihood of simulated events with comparative language: more likely, less likely, equally likely, impossible and certain. They use spinners, coins, bags and number cubes.

A simulated event uses a coin, spinner, bag or number cube to act out something real. For example, a class can toss a coin many times, with heads for a goal and tails for a miss, and record the results with tallies.

faq.q: What is the difference between likely and certain?
faq.a: Certain means it must happen every time, like Wednesday coming after Tuesday. Likely means it will probably happen but could fail, like landing on blue when 3 of 4 equal sections are blue.

faq.q: How can my child tell if a game is fair?
faq.a: A game of chance is fair when every player is equally likely to win. Check that each player has parts of the same size on the spinner, or the same number of counters or number cube faces.

sets.title: Likelihood words: impossible, unlikely, likely, certain

items.q: Today is Tuesday. Tomorrow will be Wednesday. How likely is this?
items.e: The days of the week always come in the same order. Wednesday always comes after Tuesday, so it is certain.

items.q: Jasleen is 8 years old. On her next birthday, she will turn 9. How likely is this?
items.e: Everyone gets one year older on their birthday. 8 + 1 = 9, so it is certain.

items.q: Simran lets go of a soccer ball. It will fall to the ground. How likely is this?
items.e: A ball you let go of always falls. It must happen, so it is certain.

items.q: An orca will walk down the street in Victoria. How likely is this?
items.e: Orcas live in the ocean and cannot walk. This can never happen, so it is impossible.

items.q: Next month will have 40 days. How likely is this?
items.e: A month has 28, 29, 30 or 31 days. It can never have 40 days, so it is impossible.

items.q: Owen rolls a number cube. He will roll a 7. How likely is this?
items.e: The faces show 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. There is no 7, so rolling a 7 is impossible.

items.q: It will rain at least once in Vancouver in November. How likely is this?
items.e: Vancouver gets a lot of rain in November, so it is likely. We cannot be sure, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: There will be snow on the ski hills at Whistler in January. How likely is this?
items.e: Whistler’s ski hills almost always have snow in January. But we cannot be sure, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: The next car that drives past the school will have 4 wheels. How likely is this?
items.e: Most vehicles on the road have 4 wheels. But the next one could be a motorcycle or a big truck, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: Emma will find a $20 bill on the sidewalk on the way to school. How likely is this?
items.e: It could happen, but it almost never does. So it is unlikely. It is not impossible: people do drop money.

items.q: A black bear will walk onto the school field in Kamloops today. How likely is this?
items.e: Bears do live near Kamloops, so it could happen. But it hardly ever does. So it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Lucas’s hockey team will score 20 goals in one game. How likely is this?
items.e: Hockey teams usually score only a few goals in a game. 20 goals could happen, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Hana tosses a coin. It will land on heads. How likely is this?
items.e: A coin has 2 sides: heads and tails. Heads and tails have the same chance, so it is equally likely.

items.q: Mateo hides a loonie in one of his two closed hands. Sofia picks a hand. She will pick the hand with the loonie. How likely is this?
items.e: There are 2 hands and the loonie is in 1 of them. The loonie hand and the empty hand have the same chance, so it is equally likely.

items.q: Kai says, “It is certain that it will rain in Vancouver tomorrow, because it rains there a lot.” Which word should he use instead?
items.e: Rain in Vancouver happens often, but some days are dry. It could fail to happen, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: Zara’s bag has 9 green counters and 1 yellow counter. She says, “Picking the yellow counter is impossible.” Which word should she use instead?
items.e: There is 1 yellow counter, so it could be picked. It is possible, but not very likely. The right word is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Which is more likely in Vancouver?
items.e: November is a very rainy month in Vancouver. July is summer, and snow then is almost impossible. So rain in November is more likely.

items.q: Which event is certain?
c: Ryan will see an eagle today
Next Saturday will come after Friday
It will be sunny in Kelowna tomorrow
Ava will win the class draw
items.e: Saturday always comes after Friday, so it must happen. The other events might happen, or might not.

items.q: Leah tosses a coin. Compare landing on heads and landing on tails.
items.e: A coin has one heads side and one tails side. They have the same chance, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Which is less likely: rolling a number from 1 to 6, or rolling a 6?
items.e: Every roll is a number from 1 to 6, so that is certain. A 6 is only 1 of the 6 faces, so rolling a 6 is less likely.

sets.title: Spinners and bags: the size of each part

items.q: The spinner has 4 equal sections. Which colour is the arrow most likely to land on?
items.e: 3 of the 4 equal sections are blue and only 1 is green, so blue is most likely.

items.q: Landing on yellow is ___ than landing on red.
items.e: Yellow covers 3 quarters of the spinner. Red covers only 1 quarter. Yellow has the bigger part, so it is more likely.

items.q: Which two colours are equally likely?
items.e: Green covers half of the spinner. Blue and red each cover a quarter. Blue and red have parts of the same size, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Ryan says blue is most likely, because blue has the most sections. Which colour is most likely?
items.e: Ryan counted sections, not their size. The one red section is half of the spinner. The 3 small blue sections together make only a quarter. Red is most likely.

items.q: Landing on green is …
items.e: Every section is green. The arrow must land on green, so it is certain.

items.q: Landing on yellow is …
items.e: 7 of the 8 equal sections are yellow, so yellow is likely. It is not certain, because there is 1 purple section.

items.q: Picking a green counter from this bag is …
items.e: There are only red and blue counters. There is no green counter, so it is impossible.

items.q: Picking a yellow counter from this bag is …
items.e: Only 1 of the 10 counters is yellow. It can happen, but not often, so it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Compare picking red and picking blue.
items.e: There are 4 red and 4 blue counters. The same number of each means they are equally likely.

items.q: Picking a blue counter is ___ than picking a red counter.
items.e: There are only 2 blue counters and 6 red counters. Fewer counters means less likely. It is not impossible, because there are blue counters in the bag.

items.q: Put the colours in order from most likely to least likely.
items.e: Count each colour: green 4, yellow 3, red 1. The most counters is most likely: green, yellow, red.

items.q: On which spinner is landing on blue most likely?
items.e: Compare how much of each spinner is blue. D is three quarters blue. A has 3 blue sections, but they are small: together they are less than half of the spinner.

items.q: On which spinner is landing on yellow impossible?
items.e: Spinner B has no yellow section, so yellow is impossible there. Spinner A has 1 yellow section: yellow is unlikely there, but not impossible.

items.q: From which bag is picking a red counter certain?
items.e: Bag C has only red counters, so red is certain. Bag A is likely to give red, but not certain, because it has 1 blue counter.

items.q: From which bag are blue and green equally likely?
items.e: Bag A has 3 blue and 3 green counters. The same number of each colour means they are equally likely.

items.q: Noah colours a spinner with 4 equal sections. He wants red to be likely, but not certain. How many sections should he colour red?
items.e: 3 red sections out of 4 makes red likely. 4 red sections would make red certain. 2 would make red equally likely, and 1 would make it unlikely.

items.q: Leah’s spinner has 6 equal sections: 3 blue and 3 yellow. Which sentence is true?
c: Blue and yellow are equally likely
items.e: 3 blue and 3 yellow sections of the same size cover the same amount, so blue and yellow are equally likely.

items.q: Sofia thinks the arrow will land on red, because red is her favourite colour. Which colour is the arrow more likely to land on?
items.e: A favourite colour does not change the chance. 6 of the 8 equal sections are blue and only 2 are red, so blue is more likely.

items.q: Arjun puts 4 more yellow counters into the bag. Which colour is now more likely to be picked?
items.e: Yellow: 2 + 4 = 6 counters. Red: 5 counters. 6 is more than 5, so yellow is now more likely.

items.q: How many red counters must Chloe add to make red and blue equally likely?
items.e: Red and blue are equally likely when there are the same number of each. Blue has 7. Red has 3, so add 7 − 3 = 4 red counters.

items.q: How many times did the coin land on heads?
items.e: Count the tally marks: 2 groups of 5 is 10, and 1 more makes 11.

items.q: Heads came up 2 more times than tails. Is heads more likely on a coin?
c: No, heads and tails are equally likely
items.e: A coin has one heads side and one tails side, so they are equally likely. Results are a little different each time, so 11 and 9 is a normal result.

items.q: Which colour came up least often?
c: they all came up the same
items.e: Red: 13. Blue: 7. Yellow: 4. Yellow has the fewest tally marks.

items.q: How many more times did red come up than blue?
items.e: Red 13, blue 7. How many more means subtract: 13 − 7 = 6.

items.q: How many spins were not red?
items.e: Not red means blue or yellow: 7 + 4 = 11. You can also do 24 − 13 = 11.

items.q: From these results, which colour probably covers the biggest part of Wei’s spinner?
c: all the parts are the same size
items.e: Red came up far more often than the other colours. The colour with the biggest part comes up most often, so red probably covers the biggest part.

items.q: Kai rolled a number cube 18 times. How many times did he roll a 3?
items.e: Find 3 in the Number row. The number under it in the Times row is 4.

items.q: How many times did Kai roll a number greater than 4?
items.e: Greater than 4 means 5 or 6 (not 4 itself). 5 came up 2 times and 6 came up 4 times: 2 + 4 = 6.

items.q: Mr. Singh’s class simulates soccer penalty kicks with a coin. Heads means a goal and tails means a miss. How many goals did the simulation show?
items.e: Heads stands for a goal. Heads has 2 groups of 5 and 2 more: 12 goals.

items.q: How many kicks did the class simulate altogether?
items.e: Each toss is one kick. Add the tallies: 12 + 8 = 20.

items.q: In this simulation, what does landing on tails stand for?
items.e: In a simulation, each outcome stands for something real. Here, tails stands for a miss.

items.q: Which two colours came up the same number of times?
items.e: Red: 7. Blue: 7. Green: 6. Red and blue both came up 7 times.

items.q: Owen picks a counter, writes the colour and puts it back. How many more times did he get green than purple?
items.e: Green 15, purple 10. 15 − 10 = 5.

items.q: What do the results tell you about Owen’s bag?
c: It must have only green counters
It probably has more green counters
items.e: Green came up more often, so there are probably more green counters. It cannot be only green, because purple came up 10 times.

items.q: Lucas spins a spinner 20 times. Yellow never comes up. Is landing on yellow impossible?
c: Not sure: yellow may just be unlikely
items.e: If the spinner has a small yellow part, yellow is unlikely and might not come up in 20 spins. Look at the spinner: it is impossible only if there is no yellow at all.

items.q: Hana picks a counter 10 times and puts it back each time. She gets red all 10 times. Is picking red certain?
c: Not sure: red may just be likely
items.e: If the bag has many red counters and 1 blue, red is likely and could come up 10 times in a row. Red is certain only if every counter is red.

items.q: Mei spins a red and blue spinner 30 times. She gets red 18 times. How many times did she get blue?
items.e: Every spin is red or blue. 30 − 18 = 12 times blue.

items.q: Nadia uses a spinner to simulate the weather in Nanaimo. In 20 tries she gets rain 9 times, cloud 6 times and sun the rest of the time. How many times did she get sun?
items.e: Step 1: rain and cloud: 9 + 6 = 15. Step 2: 20 − 15 = 5 times sun.

items.q: Ethan tosses a coin 10 times: H, T, T, H, T, H, H, H, T, H. How many times did he get heads?
items.e: Count each H: there are 6. There are 4 T’s, and 6 + 4 = 10 tosses.

items.q: Chloe spins 4 more times and gets blue every time. Which colour has more tallies now?
items.e: Blue: 7 + 4 = 11. Red stays at 9. 11 is more than 9, so blue has more tallies now.

items.q: Jasleen spins this spinner 20 times. About how many times should she predict red?
items.e: Red is half of the spinner, so about half of the spins should be red. Half of 20 is 10.

items.q: Harjot spins this spinner 20 times. Which prediction is best?
items.e: 3 of the 4 equal sections are blue, so blue should come up about 3 times as often as red. Blue 15 and red 5 fits best.

items.q: Olivia spins this spinner 40 times. About how many times should she predict red?
items.e: Red is 1 of 4 equal sections, so about 1 spin in every 4 is red. 40 ÷ 4 = 10.

items.q: Ji-woo spins this spinner 20 times. About how many times should she predict red?
items.e: Red covers half of the spinner, so predict red about half the time: 10 of 20. About 7 comes from thinking the 3 sections are the same size, but they are not.

items.q: Owen predicted his 20 spins. How many more times did blue come up than he predicted?
items.e: Blue: predicted 5, result 7. 7 − 5 = 2 more times.

items.q: Which colour came up less often than Owen predicted?
items.e: Red: predicted 15, result 13. 13 is less than 15. Blue came up more often than predicted.

items.q: Was Owen’s prediction a good one?
c: No, blue should never come up
No, the results must match exactly
Yes, the results were close to it
items.e: A prediction tells you about how many, not exactly how many. 13 and 7 are close to 15 and 5, so it was a good prediction.

items.q: Lucas spins this spinner 20 times. Which result would be most surprising?
items.e: Half the spinner is red and half is blue, so you expect about 10 of each. Results near 10 are normal. Red every single time is possible, but very unlikely.

items.q: Mei’s spinner has 4 equal sections. Which spinner did she most likely use?
items.e: Green came up about 3 times as often as purple, so green probably covers 3 of the 4 sections. With 4 green sections, purple would be impossible, but it came up 5 times.

items.q: Mei and Wei spin the same spinner 20 times each. Mei gets red 9 times and Wei gets red 12 times. Which sentence is true?
c: Results can be different each time
items.e: Spins happen by chance, so two experiments with the same spinner can give different results.

items.q: Ji-woo predicts 10 heads in 20 coin tosses. She gets 12 heads. Was her prediction wrong?
c: No, results are often a little different
items.e: 10 heads out of 20 is the best prediction. 12 is close to 10. Real results often differ a little.

items.q: Hana predicts that every spin will be blue. Is she right?
c: No, blue is likely, but red can still come up
items.e: 3 of the 4 equal sections are blue, so blue is likely. Red is 1 section, so red will come up sometimes. Likely is not the same as certain.

items.q: Arjun tosses a coin 5 times and gets heads every time. What about the next toss?
c: Heads and tails are still equally likely
items.e: A coin does not remember what happened before. Every toss, heads and tails are equally likely.

items.q: Nadia picks a counter and puts it back, 16 times. Which prediction is best?
items.e: 6 of the 8 counters are red: 3 times as many red as blue. Red 12 and blue 4 fits best. Red 16 and blue 0 would mean blue is impossible, but there are blue counters.

items.q: Zara predicted each number about 5 times. Which number came up the most?
items.e: Find the biggest number in the Times row: 7. It is under the number 5. (6 is the biggest number on the cube, not the one rolled most.)

items.q: Zara says 5 will always come up most, because it did this time. Is she right?
c: No, each number is equally likely
items.e: Each face of a number cube has the same chance. Next time, a different number may come up most.

items.q: Leah spins one of these spinners 40 times: green 21, purple 19. Which spinner did she most likely use?
items.e: Green and purple came up about the same number of times. Spinner C is half green and half purple. Spinner D could never give green.

items.q: Ryan spins one of these spinners 40 times: green 9, purple 31. Which spinner did he most likely use?
items.e: Purple came up about 3 times as often as green. Spinner A is 3 quarters purple and 1 quarter green. Spinner D could not give any green.

items.q: The class uses a spinner to simulate the weather in Prince George. 1 of 3 equal sections means snow. In 12 spins, about how many times should they predict snow?
items.e: Snow is 1 of 3 equal sections, so about 1 spin in every 3. 12 ÷ 3 = 4. 9 is the prediction for no snow.

items.q: Kai predicted red about 10 times in 40 spins. He got red 11 times. What should he do?
c: Say red is now more likely
Keep his prediction: 11 is close to 10
items.e: Results vary a little each time. 11 is very close to 10, so the prediction was good.

items.q: What makes a game fair?
c: Each player is equally likely to win
One player is more likely to win
items.e: A game of chance is fair when every player has the same chance to win.

items.q: Before a soccer game in Surrey, the referee tosses a coin to choose which team kicks off. Is this fair?
c: Yes, heads and tails are equally likely
items.e: A coin has one heads side and one tails side, so each team has the same chance.

items.q: Zara gets a point for red. Owen gets a point for blue. Is the game fair?
c: No, Zara is more likely to win
No, Owen is more likely to win
No, Zara is certain to win
items.e: 3 of the 4 equal sections are red and only 1 is blue. Red is more likely, so Zara has the better chance. She is not certain to win: blue can still come up.

items.q: Emma says this game is fair, because the spinner has 2 sections: red for her and blue for Liam. Is she right?
c: No, the blue part is bigger
No, the red part is bigger
items.e: Look at the size of each part, not the number of sections. Red covers 3 quarters of the spinner, so Emma is more likely to win.

items.q: Red is for Sofia and blue is for Noah. Which spinner makes the game fair?
items.e: On Spinner C, red and blue each cover half, so they are equally likely. On B and D, one colour has a bigger part.

items.q: Kai gets a point for an even number (2, 4, 6). Leah gets a point for an odd number (1, 3, 5). Is the game fair?
c: No, Leah is more likely to win
No, Kai has the bigger numbers
items.e: Kai has 3 faces and Leah has 3 faces. Every face is equally likely, so the game is fair.

items.q: Arjun gets a point for 1 or 2. Simran gets a point for 3, 4, 5 or 6. Who is more likely to win?
items.e: Simran has 4 faces and Arjun has only 2. More faces means more likely, so Simran is more likely to win.

items.q: Harjot gets a point for a 6. Jasleen gets a point for a 1. Is the game fair?
c: Yes, a 6 and a 1 are equally likely
items.e: Each face of the cube has the same chance. A 6 is not harder to roll than a 1.

items.q: Arjun gets a point for 1 or 2. Simran gets a point for 3, 4, 5 or 6. Which change makes the game fair?
items.e: Fair means each player has 3 of the 6 faces. Give 3 to Arjun: Arjun 1, 2, 3 and Simran 4, 5, 6.

items.q: Mateo wins with red and Chloe wins with blue. How many blue counters should they add to make the game fair?
items.e: Fair means the same number of red and blue counters. Red has 5 and blue has 3, so add 5 − 3 = 2 blue.

items.q: Ryan writes the names of 4 friends on cards for a draw. He writes his own name on 2 cards. Is the draw fair?
c: No, Ryan is less likely to be picked
No, Ryan is certain to be picked
No, Ryan is more likely to be picked
items.e: Ryan’s name is on 2 cards and each friend is on only 1. More cards means more likely, so the draw is not fair.

items.q: The teacher puts 24 names in a toque, one card for each student, and picks one to feed the class fish. Is this fair?
c: No, some names are impossible to pick
Yes, every student is certain to be picked
Yes, each name is equally likely
No, the first name is more likely
items.e: Each student has exactly 1 card, so every student has the same chance.

items.q: At the school fun fair, 50 raffle tickets are sold. Liam buys 1 ticket. Liam winning the raffle is …
items.e: Liam has only 1 of the 50 tickets. He could win, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Nadia’s grandma buys 40 of the 50 raffle tickets. Who is more likely to win: Nadia’s grandma or Liam with 1 ticket?
items.e: 40 tickets is far more than 1 ticket. More tickets means more likely to win, but it is still not certain.

items.q: Wei wins a prize for picking a green counter. Bag A has 3 green and 5 yellow. Bag B has 5 green and 3 yellow. Which bag should he choose?
c: either bag, they are the same
items.e: Both bags have 8 counters. Bag B has 5 green and Bag A has only 3, so green is more likely in Bag B.

items.q: The class simulates a salmon swimming up the Fraser River with a spinner: 3 equal sections say “gets past” and 1 says “stopped”. Which is more likely in the simulation?
c: the salmon is certain to get past
items.e: 3 of the 4 equal sections say gets past, so that is more likely. It is not certain, because 1 section says stopped.

items.q: Ava and Olivia play rock, paper, scissors. Ava says she always wins because she is lucky. Which is true?
c: Ava is more likely, because she is lucky
Each player is equally likely to win
items.e: When both players choose by chance, each one is equally likely to win a round. Luck does not change the chance.

items.q: Mei and Ji-woo test a game 20 times to see if it is fair. Which result shows a fair game best?
items.e: In a fair game, each player should win about half the time: about 10 each. 11 and 9 is closest.

items.q: Three friends play. Owen has red, Leah has blue and Kai has yellow. Is the game fair?
c: No, there are too many players
No, Kai is more likely to win
Yes, the 3 parts are the same size
items.e: The 3 sections are equal, so each friend has the same chance to win. The game is fair.

items.q: Owen has red, Leah has blue and Kai has yellow. Who is most likely to win?
items.e: Red covers half of the spinner. Blue and yellow each cover only a quarter. Owen’s colour has the biggest part, so he is most likely to win.
